I recently updated R and now my corrplot() code that was working before throws an error when I try and use it. Specifically, it won't work when I ask it to plot only significant variables.

Here is the old code I had:
corrplot(res3$r, order="hclust",
         p.mat = res3$P, sig.level = 0.05, insig = "blank",tl.cex=1.5)

I get the error that there are unused arguments (all arguments after res3$r are unused...?). If anyone can shed some light onto how to get this fixed that would be great!

Thanks,
Hannah

--

Hi Hannah,
One additional thought in case the previous options don't work. There may be another corrplot function masked by a different package you have installed. Explicitly calling the corrplot function from the corrplot package may help, in case there's a conflict somewhere. This is similar to a few of the dplyr functions (filter/select/summarize) that conflict with other modeling functions of the same name. To explicitly call a function from a package, we use the following:
NameOfPackage::name_of_function()
So, try using:
 corrplot::corrplot(res3$r, order="hclust",

         p.mat = res3$P, sig.level = 0.05, insig = "blank",tl.cex=1.5)

And let us know if you get a similar error.

Good luck,
Ryan

library(ggplot2)

scale_colour_discrete <- function(...) scale_colour_manual(..., values = colors_i_want)
scale_fill_discrete <- function(...) scale_fill_manual(..., values = colors_i_want)

messages.body_plain:
WHAT: a research talk!
WHO: Dr. Olga Botvinnik, Chan Zuckerberg BioHub
  (https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&user=TftcErcAAAAJ&view_op=list_works&sortby=pubdate,
https://twitter.com/olgabot)

WHERE: Data Science Initiative, 3rd Floor, Shields Library
WHEN: 1-2pm, Thursday, March 15.
HOSTS: Luiz Irber <lcir...@ucdavis.edu>, Titus Brown <ctb...@ucdavis.edu>

----

# Reference-free comparative transcriptomics

Single-cell RNA-seq is a powerful technology for identifying novel and
known cell types, however its power is limited to organisms with
well-annotated genomes. We present a reference-free method to compare
single cells both within and across species. In this method, k-mers from
each cell’s RNA-seq profile are randomly subsampled into a compressed
representation called a “sketch” using document comparison algorithms of
MinHash or HyperLogLog. For within-species comparison, the RNA sketches are
sufficient, but as protein sequence is more stable across species, we
translate the RNA k-mers into protein k-mers with 6-frame translation,
discarding all protein k-mers containing stop codons. We show this method
can “lift over” single-cell RNA-seq annotations from mouse to human and
compare to using purely 1:1 mapping orthologous genes. Thus, k-mer sketches
are an efficient method to find shared and unique cell types both within
and across species without need for a reference genome or transcriptome.

---

Cheers,
Luiz Irber

messages.body_plain:
Another approach:

You need the lat/lon of at least two points in your grid to be able to translate between grid units and degrees. E.g. 1 unit in the y direction = how many degrees?

Converting your y units to latitude should be straightforward, because the actual length of a degree latitude does not change anywhere on earth <https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616>.

delta.y = y1 - y2 # grid coordinates
delta.y.lat = y1.lat - y2.lat  # lat coordinates
gridY2lat  <- function(y) y * delta.y.lat/ delta.y
lat2gridY <- function(lat) lat * delta.y / delta.y.lat

converting your x units will be more tricky, because the linear distance of longitude degrees change depending on where you are on earth (because its a sphere). So if you are 100 ft from the north pole 1 degree longitude will be a very small distance, but if you are at the equator it will be around 1 km.

If your area of interest is relatively small (say within a few degrees, not too far from the equator), and you don't need much precision the method above should be fine for calculating x values.

Otherwise you can use a formula  <https://gis.stackexchange.com/questions/142326/calculating-longitude-length-in-miles>to find the distance of a longitude degree, given latitude:

Longitude = latitude in radians * length of degree at equator
gridX2lat <- function(x,y) {  gridY2lat(y) * pi/180  * lat2gridY(1) }

Haven't tried this out, but hopefully helpful. Also since this is not really an R question, there are probably some spatial groups at davis that could help out as well.

#maptimeDavis will meet on Tuesdays from 1:00-3:00 in the DSI Classroom (room 360 Shields Library) for Spring Quarter.  We are now accepting proposals for workshops from our community.  If you would like to present a workshop for Spring Quarter (which officially runs from April 1 to June 13), please send me an email with your proposed workshop title, a description of what you plan to teach, and which dates you would like.  We’re filling the schedule now, so please don’t wait to send your proposal.

What topics are people asking for? Here are some suggestions in no particular order:

·         Python for spatial data

·         R Spatial

·         Spatial Networks

·         Spatial Databases

·         Remote Sensing Data Sources

·         GPS

·         ArcPy

·         Matlab for spatial data

·         Statistical methods for spatial data

·         Geocoding

Can you present a different topic?  Of course!  Introductory workshops are usually popular and always needed.

Workshops should fill the 2 hour time slot and teach participants a practical skill in the general field of mapping – GIS, remote sensing, programming for spatial data, surveying, etc.  Plan for about 1.5 hours of teaching.  Both open source and proprietary software are acceptable, but participants should be able to access the necessary software either through a campus-wide license or a trial version.  We potentially have access to a computer lab with access to some proprietary software.  I’m happy to work with presenters to find access to software.

I very much appreciate everyone’s contributions to make #maptimeDavis a success!  Presenting & attending workshops is what makes this community work.  I’m happy to help presenters plan and design workshops, so please don’t hesitate to send me questions or ask for support!

hor <- read_csv("~/Downloads/hanna_output_rebeka.csv")
kht <- read_csv("~/Downloads/khThomas.csv")

fuzzy_left_join(
> kht,
> hor,
> by=c("depth"="depth1", "depth"="depth2"),
> match_fun=list(`>=`, `<=`)
)
